title: Flipped polarity: たい, potential and そう
summary: In 〜が食べたい the main carriage is the thing that makes you want it. With no such thing in the sentence, the feeling flips back to the person.

blocks.text: Every sentence has an **engine** and a **が main carriage**. Everything else tells you more about one of the two. Now look at クレープが食べたい. The carriage is **クレープ**, not "I". The engine is the helper adjective **たい**, so the sentence describes the crepes as having a quality: they stir up the wish to eat them. English puts an ego in the center ("I want"); Japanese is happy to put the thing that causes the feeling in the center.
Polarity flips when the cause is missing

Feelings can be described from the **inducer** (the crepes that stir the wish) or from the **experiencer** (the person who feels it). Japanese treats the two as halves of one event, so the default points at the inducer, but when no inducer is in the sentence the feeling swings to the person. In 東京に行きたい, 東京 already has に and 行く is a verb, so the only possible carriage is a zero: **(私が)** 東京に行きたい.
クレープが食べたい。 Crepes are eat-wanting (to me).
（私が）東京に行きたい。 (I) want to go to Tokyo.
The same flip in the potential

本が読める really says "the book does readable". The carriage is the book. But 私が読める or さくらが読める (no particular thing to read) points at the person: "I can read, I am literate". When no object is the focus, the polarity flips to the doer.

不思議そう on its own would mean "seems mysterious", but mysterious is already a feeling. In 不思議そうに言った it flips to the person: "said in a puzzled way". It describes someone who senses mystery in something.

blocks.jp: お腹が空いた。早く食べたい。
あのケーキが食べたい。
blocks.en: That cake makes (me) want to eat it.
(I) can read this kanji. (the kanji does readable)

blocks.jp: 子供は不思議そうに空を見た。
blocks.en: The child looked at the sky with a puzzled look.

items: In **Aが + 〜たい**, the thing wanted is the carriage and たい is an adjective engine.
With no inducer in the sentence, the feeling or ability points to the **person** (a zero carriage).
The potential and **〜そう** flip in the same way.
Never read が as marking an object; it only ever marks the main carriage.

questions.instruction: In ラーメンが食べたい, which word is the main carriage?
questions.note: が marks the carriage: the ramen is what stirs the wish.

questions.instruction: What kind of engine is たい?
questions.note: たい ends in い and conjugates like an adjective.
食べたい is the engine pulling the sentence.

questions.instruction: Who is the invisible carriage here?
questions.note: 京都 already has に, so the only free carriage is a zero pointing at the feeler.

questions.prompt: In 本が読める, the main carriage is the person who reads.
questions.note: The book is the carriage: the book does readable.
With no thing to read named, the potential flips to the person.

questions.instruction: Why can が not be an object marker in この本が読みたい?
options: が only ever marks the main carriage
Because たい is a verb
Because 本 is not a noun
questions.note: The book is the carriage, not an object.

questions.instruction: What does 不思議そうに言った describe?
options: A speech that cannot be heard
Something that seems strange to nobody
questions.note: そう flips here to the person feeling the mystery.

questions.instruction: Pick the sentence where the feeler is only a zero
questions.note: 家に is already に-marked and nothing else could be the carriage.

questions.prompt: (I) want to go to the sea tomorrow. (time first)
questions.note: Time, destination, then the たい engine at the end.

questions.instruction: Why does Japanese happily put the thing that causes the feeling at the center?
options: It does not need an ego at the center of every feeling
Because English works the same way
questions.note: Inducer and experiencer are two halves of one event.

questions.instruction: Which sentence points at a person's ability, not at a thing?
questions.note: Only さくら is a person; in the others the readable thing is the carriage.
